Chapter 6: Guiding Emotional Regulation Through Movement and Stillness
As kids get more comfortable with yoga’s playful routines, there’s a gentle next step—showing them how both movement and stillness can help with those big, sometimes overwhelming, feelings. Emotional regulation isn’t something we’re born knowing—it’s a skill we grow into. And yoga? It’s such a great way for children to practice calming themselves, letting out extra energy, and finding that sweet spot of balance.
So, where do we start? Well, it helps to guide kids in noticing how emotions actually show up in their bodies. Think about it—excitement might feel like wiggly legs or a heart that’s beating a mile a minute. Sadness, on the other hand, can feel heavy or slow. One of the most powerful things adults can do is use simple, clear language to connect those feelings with what’s happening physically. You might ask, “When you feel mad, do your fists get tight?” Or, “When you’re happy, do you want to jump?” It’s all about making those connections.
Yoga offers a whole toolkit for handling these sensations. Here’s how you can help:
For kids bursting with energy—maybe they’re excited or frustrated—try active movement. Jumping, shaking out their arms, or stretching tall can help release all that built-up energy.
For moments of sadness or when a child feels tired, gentle stretching and slow, flowing movements can feel soothing, almost like a comforting hug.
And when things feel just too overwhelming? Stillness is a wonderful option. Curling up like a rock, or lying quietly on the mat, can help reset the nervous system and bring a sense of calm.
The magic really happens when children are encouraged to play around with different movements and notice what helps them feel better. Some kids, when they’re anxious, might love hugging their knees to their chest. Others might find it calming to sway side to side. As an adult, your role is to offer options, celebrate their choices, and let each child’s unique experience be valid.
And let’s not forget about the breath. When emotions are running high, bringing attention back to the breath—maybe through a favorite breathing game—can make all the difference. It gives kids a sense of control and safety, reminding them that their breath is always there to help.
Over time, children start to realize that movement and stillness aren’t just things they do—they’re actual tools for navigating tough feelings, instead of just being swept away by them.
Want a few practical strategies to try?
Start with emotion-matching poses. Choose movements that reflect or gently shift a feeling—like stomping like an elephant when you’re angry, or floating like a cloud when you’re calm.
Build in pause-and-breathe moments. Encourage kids to take a quiet breath before they react, giving themselves a little space to decide what comes next.
And set up safe spaces for stillness. Maybe there’s a cozy corner, or a soft mat that’s always available for some quiet time whenever it’s needed.
By weaving these small practices into everyday routines, children slowly build up resilience and self-awareness. They start to understand that all feelings are okay—and more importantly, that they have choices in how they respond.
